title: Claude Code & the evolution of agentic coding — Boris Cherny, Anthropic

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary object is Claude Code, a coding agent for software engineering, covering its design philosophy, interfaces, and practical agentic coding workflows. Claude Code is an IDE/terminal coding assistant used by software developers for code generation, review, and engineering tasks. Covers development-time usage (coding, planning, TDD, context management) and production usage (GitHub Actions, parallel multi-Claude instances). Requires familiarity with software development practices and AI tooling but is accessible to practicing engineers. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. summary:
Boris Cherny opens by noting the audience's familiarity with Claude Code and frames his talk as a zoomed-out view of the coding space, the UX of coding, and Claude Code's approach. His central thesis is that the model is on an exponential improvement curve for coding ability, but the product is struggling to keep up—Anthropic feels it is building the bare minimum because it does not yet know the ideal product UX. Claude Code is intentionally unopinionated and simple to let users experience the model in a raw, low-level way and to learn what works.

Boris traces the history of programming from physical switchboards (1930s–40s) to punch cards (1950s–70s), through rising abstraction: assembly, COBOL, typed languages, C++, and 1990s language families. He notes modern languages have largely converged in feel. He then traces the UX of programming: the IBM 029 keypunch, Ken Thompson's Ed, Vim/Emacs, Smalltalk-80 (first graphical interface with live reload), Visual Basic (1991), Eclipse (static-analysis type ahead), Copilot (AI type ahead), and Devon (natural language to code). Verification evolved from manual debugging to probabilistic methods like fuzzing and chaos testing.

Claude Code's approach differs: start with the terminal, give low-level model access, stay productive, unopinionated, and out of the way. The more general model always wins, and everything around the model also improves exponentially. He outlines four usage modes: terminal, IDE integration (deliberately less polished than Cursor/Windsurf), GitHub integration (runs on user's compute, data stays local, one slash command), and the SDK (claude -p, pipable like a Unix utility, ~10% explored).

Boris then shares practical tips. At Anthropic, codebase Q&A via Claude Code shortened engineer onboarding from 2-3 weeks to ~2 days. He uses Claude to summarize his git commits for weekly standups. He recommends teaching Claude your tools by running claude --help, putting the results in CLAUDE.md—no plugin or extension needed; MCP works for fancier needs. Effective workflows include having Claude explore and plan before coding (now formalized as plan mode via shift+tab, launched today), using TDD (write tests first, tell Claude they won't pass yet, commit, then write code and commit), and giving Claude iteration targets (unit tests, screenshots, even a camera on a 3D printer). Extended thinking works best when Claude already has context, not up front. For more context, use CLAUDE.md files in the repo root, subfolders, or home folder; markdown files in a commands folder become slash commands; typing # lets you ask Claude to memorize things. Power users run multiple Claude instances in parallel across terminal tabs, git work trees, or GitHub Actions; for coordination between instances, have each write to a markdown file.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The model is improving at coding exponentially; the product layer struggles to keep up, and Anthropic is building the bare minimum while learning the right UX.
Claude Code is intentionally unopinionated, simple, and terminal-first to expose the model in a raw, low-level way.
Claude Code is available via four interfaces: terminal, IDE integration, GitHub app (user's own compute, data local), and a programmatic SDK (claude -p, pipable like a Unix utility, ~10% explored).
Codebase Q&A is the simplest onboarding entry point—at Anthropic it reduced engineer onboarding from 2-3 weeks to ~2 days.
Teach Claude your tools by running claude --help and putting results in CLAUDE.md—no plugin or extension needed; MCP works for fancier functionality.
Effective workflows: have Claude plan before coding (plan mode via shift+tab), use TDD, and give Claude iteration targets like tests or screenshots.
Extended thinking works best when Claude already has context from tool use; thinking up front wastes tokens.
CLAUDE.md files (repo root, subfolders, home), slash commands from markdown files, and # memorize provide scalable context management.
Power users run multiple Claude instances in parallel across terminal tabs, git work trees, or GitHub Actions; coordination via markdown files.
Memory UX is a new concept for coding models that did not exist in previous IDEs—Anthropic is iterating on it and wants feedback.

sections.title: Introduction and TL;DR
sections.summary: Boris introduces himself as creator of Claude Code. His thesis: the model improves exponentially at coding, the product struggles to keep up, and Claude Code stays unopinionated because the right UX is unknown.

sections.title: Getting Claude Code
sections.summary: Boris explains installation via claude.ai/code and npm, noting support for Claude Pro (as of yesterday) and Claude Max.

sections.title: Evolution of programming languages
sections.summary: Traces programming from physical switchboards to punch cards to assembly, COBOL, C++, and 1990s language families, noting modern languages have converged in feel.

sections.title: UX of programming tools
sections.summary: Traces UX from IBM 029 keypunch, to Ed (first text editor by Ken Thompson), Vim/Emacs, Smalltalk-80 (graphical + live reload), Visual Basic (1991 graphical mainstream), Eclipse (static type ahead), Copilot (AI type ahead), and Devon (natural language to code).

sections.title: Verification evolution
sections.summary: Verification moved from manual debugging and physical inspection to probabilistic methods like fuzzing, vulnerability testing, and Netflix chaos testing.

sections.title: Claude Code's approach and philosophy
sections.summary: Claude Code starts with the terminal, gives low-level model access, stays unopinionated and out of the way. The more general model always wins; everything around the model also improves exponentially.

sections.title: Claude Code interfaces: terminal, IDE, GitHub, SDK
sections.summary: Four usage modes: terminal (any terminal), IDE (in-IDE diffs, diagnostics), GitHub app (user's compute, data local, one slash command), and SDK (claude -p, Unix-utility pipable, ~10% explored).

sections.title: Tips: codebase Q&A and onboarding
sections.summary: Codebase Q&A is the simplest onboarding for new users. At Anthropic it reduced engineer onboarding from 2-3 weeks to ~2 days. Boris uses Claude to summarize git commits for weekly standups.

sections.title: Tips: teach Claude your tools
sections.summary: New coding tools can use all your existing tools—bash tools, MCP tools—without building extensions. Run claude --help, put results in CLAUDE.md. MCP works for fancier functionality like streaming.

sections.title: Tips: effective workflows
sections.summary: Have Claude explore and plan before writing code. Extended thinking works best after context is loaded, not up front. TDD works well with agents: write tests first, tell Claude they won't pass, commit, then write code and commit. Give Claude iteration targets (unit tests, screenshots, even a 3D printer camera)—first shot is okay, second or third is much better.

sections.title: Tips: plan mode and context management
sections.summary: Plan mode launched today via shift+tab—Claude makes a plan and waits for approval. CLAUDE.md files in repo root, subfolders, and home folder provide context. Markdown files in a commands folder become slash commands. Typing # asks Claude to memorize something. Memory UX is new to coding models and still rough but being iterated.

sections.title: Q&A: parallel usage
sections.summary: Power users multi-Claude: multiple terminal tabs with different checkouts or git work trees, or GitHub Actions for parallel work. Coordination usually isn't needed; if it is, have each Claude write to a markdown file.
